pos: n. (the first of the three monastic vows: the renunciation of personal and, in the stricter orders, corporate property)
etymology: Latin votum, a thing vowed, from vovere, to vow; with paupertas, poverty, from pauper, poor.
biblical_def: The vow of poverty is the renunciation of private property, sworn for life, and in the mendicant orders extended to the house itself. Scripture treats vows with great seriousness, and so must any assessment of this one. “If a man vow a vow unto the LORD, or swear an oath to bind his soul with a bond; he shall not break his word” (Num 30:2) makes a vow binding; “Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay” (Ecc 5:5) warns against making one lightly. So a man who has sworn poverty is bound, and the Reformers' release of monks from their vows rested not on the triviality of vowing but on the claim that the vow itself was unlawfully made — a promise of what God had not required, binding a conscience God had left free. That is the heart of the matter. Scripture commends generosity, warns incessantly against covetousness, and records the Jerusalem church holding “all things common” (Act 4:32) as a free act of love, not a vow. “Whiles it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power?” (Act 5:4) — Peter's words to Ananias establish that property remained the giver's to dispose, which is the opposite of a vow.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vow as a solemn promise made to God, and poverty as destitution of property, indigence; renunciation as the act of disowning or disclaiming; and property as the exclusive right of possessing and disposing of a thing.
webster_full: VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God, or by a pagan to his deity; a solemn promise whereby a man binds himself to do or to forbear something.
VOW, v.t. To give, consecrate or dedicate to God by a solemn promise.
POVERTY, n. Destitution of property; indigence; want of convenient means of subsistence.
RENUNCIATION, n. The act of renouncing; a disowning; rejection; the declining to own or acknowledge as belonging to one's self.
PROPERTY, n. The exclusive right of possessing, enjoying and disposing of a thing; ownership.
scriptures: Num 30:2
If a man vow a vow unto the LORD, or swear an oath to bind his soul with a bond; he shall not break his word, he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth.
Ecc 5:5
Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.
Act 4:32
And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common.
Act 5:4
Whiles it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power? why hast thou conceived this thing in thine heart? thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God.
corruption_summary: The sworn renunciation of property: a vow God never required, binding where he left the conscience free, and generosity turned into merit.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is twofold and both halves matter. First, the vow binds where Scripture does not bind, and Paul calls such self-imposed ordinances the mark of a religion of the flesh: “why, as though living in the world, are ye subject to ordinances” (Col 2:20), “Touch not; taste not; handle not” (Col 2:21). Second, it attaches merit to the renunciation, which turns an act of love into a transaction and leaves the poor man a creditor of God.

The modern misuse is to read every criticism of this vow as a defence of accumulation. It is not. The principle to recover is free, costly, unvowed generosity: “let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth” (Eph 4:28) — a man who works in order to have something to give is doing more than a man who has sworn to have nothing.
roots_summary: Hebrew neder (H5088), a vow; Hebrew asar (H631), to bind; Greek euche (G2171), a vow; Greek ptocheia (G4432), poverty; Greek koinos (G2839), common.
roots_lines: Hebrew neder (H5088) — a vow, a votive offering; “Vow, and pay unto the LORD your God” (Psa 76:11).
Hebrew asar (H631) — to bind, to tie; “to bind his soul with a bond” (Num 30:2).
Greek euche (G2171) — a vow; the New Testament keeps the Old Testament's weight upon it.
Greek koinos (G2839) — common, shared; “but they had all things common” (Act 4:32) — freely, not by oath.
Greek ptocheia (G4432) — destitution; used of Christ's self-emptying, never as a human credit.
usage: “Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay” (Ecc 5:5) — why a rash vow is worse than none.
“was it not in thine own power?” (Act 5:4) — property left in the owner's hands, which a vow removes.
“Touch not; taste not; handle not” (Col 2:21) — Paul's summary of self-imposed renunciation.

pos: n. (the second monastic vow: perpetual celibacy, sworn for life)
etymology: Latin castitas, purity, from castus, pure or chaste; with votum, a vow.
biblical_def: The vow of chastity is sworn lifelong celibacy. Scripture does recognise a genuine gift of singleness, and recognises that it frees a man for undistracted service: “He that is unmarried careth for the things that belong to the Lord, how he may please the Lord” (1Co 7:32), and Christ's own words, “there be eunuchs, which have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven's sake” (Mat 19:12). But the same passages hedge the gift about with cautions a vow cannot honour. “All men cannot receive this saying, save they to whom it is given” (Mat 19:11) makes it a gift, not an undertaking; “every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that” (1Co 7:7) refuses to rank the two; and Paul's plain provision for the man who finds he lacks the gift is marriage: “if they cannot contain, let them marry: for it is better to marry than to burn” (1Co 7:9). A vow forecloses that remedy for life, on the strength of a young man's estimate of himself. Worse, by elevating celibacy to a higher estate it slanders marriage, which Scripture declares “honourable in all” (Heb 13:4) without qualification.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines chastity as purity of the body, freedom from all unlawful commerce of sexes, and in a single person continence; celibacy as single life, the state of an unmarried person; and marriage as the act of uniting a man and woman for life.
webster_full: CHASTITY, n. Purity of the body; freedom from all unlawful commerce of sexes. Before marriage, purity from all commerce of sexes; after marriage, fidelity to the marriage bed.
CELIBACY, n. An unmarried state; a single life. It is most frequently applied to the single state of males.
CONTINENCE, n. In a general sense, the restraint which a person imposes upon his desires and passions; chastity.
MARRIAGE, n. The act of uniting a man and woman for life; wedlock; the legal union of a man and woman for life.
HONOURABLE, a. Worthy of honor; illustrious; noble; conferring honor; consistent with honor or reputation.
scriptures: But I would have you without carefulness. He that is unmarried careth for the things that belong to the Lord, how he may please the Lord:

For there are some eunuchs, which were so born from their mother's womb: and there are some eunuchs, which were made eunuchs of men: and there be eunuchs, which have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven's sake. He that is able to receive it, let him receive it.
But if they cannot contain, let them marry: for it is better to marry than to burn.
Heb 13:4
Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.
corruption_summary: Sworn lifelong celibacy: a real gift turned into a binding undertaking, and a higher estate invented at the expense of marriage.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is doctrinal and Paul names it among the gravest. Teaching that forbids marriage he assigns not to zeal but to deception: “in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils” (1Ti 4:1), “Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:3). A rule requiring celibacy of all clergy is in exactly that line, and the pastoral wreckage it has produced across centuries is the predictable fruit of binding what God left free. Scripture's own qualification for an overseer assumes the opposite: “A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife” (1Ti 3:2).

The modern misuse runs the other way: a culture that cannot imagine continence at all, and treats the unmarried Christian as deprived by definition. That is its own error. The principle to recover is Paul's balance — singleness is a real gift with real freedom, marriage is honourable in all, neither is a rank, and no man should swear away a remedy God has provided: “not that I may cast a snare upon you” (1Co 7:35).
roots_summary: Greek hagneia (G47), purity; Greek egkrateia (G1466), self-control; Greek charisma (G5486), a gift of grace; Greek gameo (G1060), to marry; Hebrew tahor (H2889), clean.
roots_lines: Greek hagneia (G47) — purity, chastity; a quality required of every Christian, married or not.
Greek egkrateia (G1466) — self-control; “But if they cannot contain, let them marry” (1Co 7:9) turns on the lack of it.
Greek charisma (G5486) — a gift of grace; “every man hath his proper gift of God” (1Co 7:7).
Greek gameo (G1060) — to marry; “Forbidding to marry” (1Ti 4:3) is what Paul calls a doctrine of devils.
Hebrew tahor (H2889) — clean, pure; purity in Scripture is of the heart first, and of the body as its expression.
usage: “All men cannot receive this saying, save they to whom it is given” (Mat 19:11) — a gift, which no vow can confer.
“Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled” (Heb 13:4) — the clause that forbids a higher estate.
“Forbidding to marry” (1Ti 4:3) — the apostolic verdict on a compulsory rule.

pos: n. (the third monastic vow: submission of the will to the abbot or superior as to Christ)
etymology: Latin obedientia, from obedire, to give ear or hearken, from ob, toward, and audire, to hear. Obedience is first a hearing.
biblical_def: The vow of obedience binds a monk to his abbot — in Benedict's rule, to obey him as Christ, without delay and without murmuring. Scripture does command submission to those set over us in the Lord: “Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account” (Heb 13:17), and “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1). Obedience to legitimate authority is a Christian duty and the modern instinct against all authority is not a virtue. But the vow goes past what Scripture asks in two ways. It makes the submission total and lifelong, whereas every command to obey a man is bounded by the higher claim — “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). And it transfers the conscience, which cannot be transferred: a brother who obeys a wrong order is not thereby innocent. Scripture's own ordering is instructive. Obedience to God is a hearing of his voice — “Obey my voice, and I will be your God” (Jer 7:23) — and “to obey is better than sacrifice” (1Sa 15:22) sets obedience above every offering, including the offering of one's own will to a superior.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines obedience as compliance with a command or prohibition, the performance of what is required by authority; submission as the act of yielding to power or authority; and superior as one who is more advanced in rank or office.
webster_full: OBEDIENCE, n. Compliance with a command, prohibition or known law and rule prescribed; submission to authority.
OBEY, v.t. To comply with the commands, orders or instructions of a superior; to do what one is commanded.
SUBMISSION, n. The act of submitting; the yielding of one's person to the power or authority of another; obedience.
SUPERIOR, n. One who is more advanced in rank or office; the chief of a monastery or convent.
CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong; the faculty or principle which decides on the lawfulness or unlawfulness of our actions.
scriptures: Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
And Samuel said, Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.
Jer 7:23
But this thing commanded I them, saying, Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and ye shall be my people: and walk ye in all the ways that I have commanded you, that it may be well unto you.
corruption_summary: Total lifelong submission to a superior: obedience is a duty, but a vow that transfers the conscience asks what no man may give.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the transfer of conscience. A vow to obey a man as Christ, without delay and without question, removes the one check Scripture insists on keeping: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). Peter said it to the highest ecclesiastical court of his day. Any system of obedience that cannot accommodate that sentence has made an idol of its own order, however pious its intention.

The modern corruption is the mirror image: a suspicion of all authority that treats every command as an imposition and every submission as weakness. Scripture is against both. The principle to recover is bounded, glad submission — “that they may do it with joy, and not with grief” (Heb 13:17) puts a duty on the one who obeys and names the limit by naming the end: the watching of souls, not the convenience of the superior.
roots_summary: Hebrew shama (H8085), to hear and obey; Greek hupakouo (G5219), to listen under; Greek hupotasso (G5293), to place under; Greek peitharcheo (G3980), to obey authority; Hebrew qashab (H7181), to incline the ear.
roots_lines: Hebrew shama (H8085) — to hear, and so to obey; “Obey my voice, and I will be your God” (Jer 7:23).
Greek hupakouo (G5219) — to hearken under, to obey; “Children, obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right” (Eph 6:1).
Greek hupotasso (G5293) — to arrange under, to submit; “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1).
Greek peitharcheo (G3980) — to obey one in authority; the word Peter's refusal before the council stands against.
Hebrew qashab (H7181) — to prick up the ear, attend closely; the posture obedience begins in.
usage: “to obey is better than sacrifice” (1Sa 15:22) — obedience above every offering, including a surrendered will.
“We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — the limit no vow may erase.
“for they watch for your souls” (Heb 13:17) — the reason for submission, and so its boundary.

pos: n. pl. (in Roman theology, poverty, chastity and obedience: counsels held to be advised rather than commanded, and to constitute a higher state of perfection)
etymology: Greek euaggelion, gospel, through Latin evangelicus; with Latin consilium, counsel or advice, as distinguished from praeceptum, a precept.
biblical_def: The evangelical counsels are poverty, chastity and obedience, classified in Roman theology as counsels rather than precepts: not commanded of all, but advised to those seeking perfection. The distinction between precept and counsel is the architecture of the whole two-tier system, and it is the point a Protestant must contest, because on it rests the claim that some Christians are more Christian than others. Scripture does not recognise the division. The law's demand is total and binds every man — “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind” (Mat 22:37) leaves no residue of optional excellence to add. What Christ said to one rich young man he said to expose that man's idol, and Scripture draws the lesson about riches generally, not about a vocation for the few. Nor is perfection an attainment of a class: “Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after” (Phi 3:12) is Paul, late in life, about himself. The counsels doctrine is therefore not a harmless taxonomy. It produces a church of two estates and a laity taught to expect less of itself than God requires of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines counsel as advice, opinion or instruction given upon request; precept as any commandment or order intended as an authoritative rule of action; and perfection as the state of being complete or without defect.
webster_full: COUNSEL, n. Advice; opinion, or instruction, given upon request or otherwise, for directing the judgment or conduct of another.
PRECEPT, n. Any commandment or order intended as an authoritative rule of action; a mandate; a rule of moral conduct.
PERFECTION, n. The state of being perfect or complete, so that nothing requisite is wanting; also, a quality, endowment or acquirement completely excellent.
EVANGELICAL, a. According to the gospel; consonant to the doctrines of the gospel; sound in the doctrines of the gospel.
STATE, n. Condition; the circumstances of a being or thing at any given time; also, rank; condition; quality.
scriptures: Jesus said unto him, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind.
Phi 3:12
Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus.
So likewise ye, when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do.
Gal 3:10
For as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse: for it is written, Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them.
corruption_summary: Poverty, chastity and obedience classed as advice rather than command: the doctrine that builds two tiers of Christian and lowers what is asked of the laity.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the precept-and-counsel scheme itself. If the law is fully satisfied by precepts, a man may have works to spare, and from that surplus grow merit, supererogation and the treasury of the church. Christ closes the door: “when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do” (Luk 17:10). There is no surplus. And the law's claim is not partial but entire: “Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them” (Gal 3:10).

The modern version of the same error is subtler and thrives in Protestant churches: a tier of the radical, the sold-out, the missionary, against whom the ordinary believer measures himself short. The principle to recover is that there is one standard, it is total, nobody meets it, and Christ has met it for his people. “with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind” (Mat 22:37) is addressed to everyone, and it leaves no room for a higher calling.
roots_summary: Greek euaggelion (G2098), gospel; Latin consilium, counsel; Greek entole (G1785), a commandment; Greek teleios (G5046), complete; Greek achreios (G888), unprofitable.
roots_lines: Latin consilium and praeceptum — counsel and command; the distinction the whole scheme rests on.
Greek entole (G1785) — a commandment; in Scripture every moral demand is one of these, never mere advice.
Greek teleios (G5046) — complete, whole, mature; “either were already perfect: but I follow after” (Phi 3:12).
Greek achreios (G888) — useless, unprofitable; “We are unprofitable servants” (Luk 17:10).
Greek euaggelion (G2098) — gospel; a word badly used in this phrase, since these counsels are law and not good news.
usage: “we have done that which was our duty to do” (Luk 17:10) — the sentence that abolishes a surplus of merit.
“Not as though I had already attained” (Phi 3:12) — Paul declining the higher estate.
“Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things” (Gal 3:10) — the law's totality, which leaves nothing optional.

pos: n. (the public act by which a novice takes the vows for life and is received into the community)
etymology: Latin professio, a public declaration, from profiteri, to declare openly; with monasticus, of a monk, from Greek monos, alone.
biblical_def: Monastic profession is the ceremony of binding: after a probationary year, the novice declares his vows publicly, often prostrate before the altar, is clothed in the habit of the professed, and in some uses is reckoned dead to the world with a funeral rite. The public character of it is not the problem; Scripture has plenty of public covenanting, and “I will go into thy house with burnt offerings: I will pay thee my vows” (Psa 66:13) is a man paying vows before witnesses. The problem is the content and the finality. A profession that is irrevocable for life, made at perhaps nineteen, concerning gifts the professed cannot yet know he has, converts a hope into a chain. And the language of dying to the world, borrowed from baptism, quietly displaces baptism: the real Christian profession was already made at the font and at the Lord's table, and it binds every believer to the same death and the same life. “we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life” (Rom 6:4) leaves no second and higher profession to make.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines profession as open declaration, public avowal of one's sentiments, and the act of entering into a religious order; novice as one newly admitted to a monastery during probation; and probation as trial, examination, proof.
webster_full: PROFESSION, n. Open declaration; public avowal or acknowledgment of one's sentiments or belief; as professions of friendship or sincerity.
PROFESSION, n. The act of entering into a religious order, and taking the vows of that order.
PROFESS, v.t. To make open declaration of; to avow or acknowledge; to declare in strong terms.
NOVICE, n. One who is new in any business; a beginner; also, one newly received into a monastery, during the time of probation.
PROBATION, n. The act of proving; proof; trial; also, moral trial; the state of a person in which he has opportunity to prove his character.
scriptures: I will go into thy house with burnt offerings: I will pay thee my vows,
Rom 6:4
Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.
Ecc 5:4
When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed.
The like figure whereunto even baptism doth also now save us (not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God,) by the resurrection of Jesus Christ:
corruption_summary: The ceremony of life vows: a second profession laid over baptism, made young and made irrevocable, binding gifts a novice cannot yet know he has.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the displacement of baptism. Scripture knows one initiation into the death and life of Christ, and it is the font: “The like figure whereunto even baptism doth also now save us (not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God,)” (1Pe 3:21). A second, higher, more binding profession teaches the professed that his baptism was a lesser thing and teaches the unprofessed that it was. Both lessons are false.

The second corruption is the finality. “When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools” (Ecc 5:4) means a vow once made is owed — which is exactly why Scripture counsels caution in making one, and why binding a youth for life to three vows is a grave thing to do to a conscience. The principle to recover is that baptism is the Christian's profession, sufficient and unrepeatable, and nothing may be laid over it.
roots_summary: Latin professio, open declaration; Greek homologia (G3671), confession; Hebrew neder (H5088), a vow; Greek baptisma (G908), baptism; Greek dokimazo (G1381), to prove or test.
roots_lines: Latin professio — a public declaration; the ceremony takes its name from the open avowal.
Greek homologia (G3671) — confession, a saying the same thing; the New Testament word for Christian profession.
Hebrew neder (H5088) — a vow; “I will pay thee my vows” (Psa 66:13).
Greek baptisma (G908) — baptism; “we are buried with him by baptism into death” (Rom 6:4).
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test, to prove; “let these also first be proved” (1Ti 3:10) — the sound instinct behind a probation.
usage: “even so we also should walk in newness of life” (Rom 6:4) — the profession already made at baptism.
“pay that which thou hast vowed” (Ecc 5:4) — why the ceremony is so weighty a thing to impose.
“And let these also first be proved” (1Ti 3:10) — testing before office, which the novitiate rightly imitated.

pos: n. (one offered or dedicated to a monastery; in early practice, a child given by his parents to be raised and professed)
etymology: Latin oblatus, offered up, past participle of offerre, to offer; the oblate is literally an offering.
biblical_def: An oblate is one offered to a monastery. In the earliest and harshest usage, this meant a child — often as young as five — handed over by his parents, raised in the cloister, and professed as a monk when he came of age, with no meaningful consent of his own. Later the word softened to mean a layman attached to a house without full vows. The practice of child oblation was defended from Hannah's offering of Samuel: “Therefore also I have lent him to the LORD; as long as he liveth he shall be lent to the LORD” (1Sa 1:28). But Hannah gave a child she had asked for and received by promise, to a service God had instituted, and Samuel grew up to a prophetic office God himself confirmed. That is not a warrant for disposing of a child's whole life to a human rule. Scripture lays the duty of a child's nurture on the parents, in the home: “thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house” (Deu 6:7) and “ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord” (Eph 6:4). A household is not to be outsourced, and a vow is not to be sworn by proxy.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines oblate in its geometrical sense as flattened at the poles, and oblation as any thing offered or presented in worship; offer as to present for acceptance or rejection; and dedicate as to set apart and consecrate to a divine Being.
webster_full: OBLATION, n. Any thing offered or presented in worship or sacred service; an offering; a sacrifice.
OBLATE, a. Flattened or depressed at the poles; as, the earth is an oblate spheroid.
OFFER, v.t. To present for acceptance or rejection; to exhibit something that may be taken or received or not; also, to present in worship.
DEDICATE, v.t. To set apart and consecrate to a divine Being, or to a sacred purpose; to devote to a sacred use.
NURTURE, n. That which nourishes; food; diet; also, education; instruction; the discipline of a child.
scriptures: Therefore also I have lent him to the LORD; as long as he liveth he shall be lent to the LORD. And he worshipped the LORD there.
Deu 6:7
And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
Eph 6:4
And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward.
corruption_summary: A person offered to a monastery — at first a young child, professed without consent: a vow sworn by proxy and a household's duty handed to an institution.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption of child oblation is grave, and it is worth stating plainly rather than softening because it is old. A boy of five cannot vow poverty, chastity and obedience, and parents cannot vow them for him; the system nonetheless held him bound, and medieval canonists argued at length about whether he might ever leave. Scripture treats children as a trust, not a currency: “Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward” (Psa 127:3) — a reward received, not an offering to be transferred.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the irreplaceable duty of the Christian household. “bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord” (Eph 6:4) is addressed to fathers, and no institution — cloister, school or programme — may be given what it names, however devout the intention of the giving.
roots_summary: Latin oblatus, offered; Hebrew sha'al (H7592), to ask or lend; Hebrew nachalah (H5159), an inheritance; Greek paideia (G3809), nurture or training; Greek prosphora (G4376), an offering.
roots_lines: Latin oblatus — offered up; the oblate is named as a thing presented.
Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — an inheritance, a heritage; “children are an heritage of the LORD” (Psa 127:3).
Greek paideia (G3809) — training, nurture, instruction; “the nurture and admonition of the Lord” (Eph 6:4).
Greek prosphora (G4376) — an offering; used of Christ's own self-offering, which is why the word sits badly on a child.
Hebrew sha'al (H7592) — to ask, and so to lend; “I have lent him to the LORD” (1Sa 1:28).
usage: “as long as he liveth he shall be lent to the LORD” (1Sa 1:28) — the text used to justify oblation, in a case unlike it.
“thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children” (Deu 6:7) — the duty that cannot be delegated.
“Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD” (Psa 127:3) — a trust, not an offering to transfer.

pos: n. (the distinctive dress of a religious order: tunic, belt, scapular and cowl, varying by rule)
etymology: Latin habitus, bearing, dress or condition, from habere, to have or hold; the habit is what one habitually wears and so what one is held to be.
biblical_def: The monastic habit is the dress of an order: a tunic, a belt or cord, a scapular, and a hood or cowl, differing by rule — black for Benedictines, undyed white for Cistercians, grey or brown for the friars. It served real purposes. It marked a man as under obedience, abolished the display of rank that clothing otherwise carries, and cost almost nothing, which is itself a rebuke: Scripture is sharp about dress as a vehicle of vanity, “that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array” (1Ti 2:9), and “the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price” (1Pe 3:4). There is biblical precedent for plain prophetic dress: Elijah was “an hairy man, and girt with a girdle of leather about his loins” (2Ki 1:8), and John the Baptist “had his raiment of camel's hair, and a leathern girdle about his loins” (Mat 3:4). The danger is equally biblical and Zechariah names it exactly: a rough garment can be worn to deceive. Dress that signals holiness will sooner or later be worn by men who want the signal without the thing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines habit as dress, garments, clothes, and also a state of mind formed by repeated acts; raiment as clothing in general, vestments; and apparel as clothing, vesture, garments.
webster_full: HABIT, n. Garb; dress; also, a garment; a coat; the dress of a particular order of persons, as the habit of a monk or a nun.
HABIT, n. A disposition or condition of the mind or body acquired by custom or a frequent repetition of the same act.
RAIMENT, n. Clothing in general; vestments; vesture; garments.
APPAREL, n. Clothing; vesture; garments; dress; also, external habiliments or decorations.
MODEST, a. Not forward or bold; not presumptuous or arrogant; also, moderate; not excessive or extreme.
scriptures: In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
And they answered him, He was an hairy man, and girt with a girdle of leather about his loins. And he said, It is Elijah the Tishbite.
Mat 3:4
And the same John had his raiment of camel's hair, and a leathern girdle about his loins; and his meat was locusts and wild honey.
corruption_summary: The dress of an order: genuine plainness and the abolition of rank, carrying the standing temptation of a garment that advertises holiness.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the garment worn to be seen, and Scripture names it twice with precision. Zechariah foresees false prophets who will no longer “wear a rough garment to deceive” (Zec 13:4), and Christ indicts the religious dress of his own day: “all their works they do for to be seen of men: they make broad their phylacteries, and enlarge the borders of their garments” (Mat 23:5). A habit that announces its wearer's sanctity is a standing invitation to the sin it was designed to cure.

The modern inversion is studied scruffiness as its own display, which is the same vanity in reverse. The principle to recover is clothing as modest, cheap and unremarkable — and the real garment Scripture tells a Christian to put on: “put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof” (Rom 13:14), and “bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering” (Col 3:12).
roots_summary: Latin habitus, dress or bearing; Hebrew beged (H899), a garment; Hebrew addereth (H155), a mantle; Greek himation (G2440), a garment; Greek enduo (G1746), to put on.
roots_lines: Latin habitus — bearing, dress, condition; the one word carries both a coat and a character.
Hebrew beged (H899) — a garment; “Take away the filthy garments from him” (Zec 3:4).
Hebrew addereth (H155) — a mantle or wide cloak; Elijah's and the prophets' rough dress.
Greek himation (G2440) — an outer garment; “enlarge the borders of their garments” (Mat 23:5).
Greek enduo (G1746) — to put on, to clothe oneself; “put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom 13:14).
usage: “neither shall they wear a rough garment to deceive” (Zec 13:4) — the exact hazard of a holy uniform.
“girt with a girdle of leather about his loins” (2Ki 1:8) — plain prophetic dress, with no order behind it.
“Put on therefore, as the elect of God” (Col 3:12) — the garments actually commanded.

pos: n. (the hood of a monastic habit; by extension the hooded outer garment worn in choir)
etymology: Latin cucullus, a hood or cap, through Old English cugele; the cowl is the hood, and later the whole hooded gown.
biblical_def: The cowl is the hood of the monastic habit, and in strict usage the wide hooded gown worn in choir over the tunic. It is the most recognisable piece of religious dress in Europe and gave the language a proverb — that the cowl does not make the monk — which is sound theology in six words and older than the Reformation. The hood had plain uses: warmth in an unheated church at two in the morning, and a means of covering the face so that a man in choir was neither seen nor seeing. That second use points to something Christ actually commands. “when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret” (Mat 6:6) asks for exactly the concealment a cowl provides, and “when thou fastest, anoint thine head, and wash thy face” (Mat 6:17) asks that devotion not be advertised. The irony is that the garment adopted to hide a man became the clearest public badge of his holiness, so that the hood meant to conceal piety ended by proclaiming it. That reversal is the whole history of religious dress in one object.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cowl as a monk's hood, usually a cap with a hood, and also a vessel; hood as a covering for the head; and secret as kept from the knowledge of others, concealed, private.
webster_full: COWL, n. A monk's hood, usually of a dark color; a cap with a hood, worn by monks of certain orders.
COWLED, a. Wearing a cowl; hooded; shaped like a cowl.
HOOD, n. A covering for the head; also, the cowl of a monk; an ornamental fold worn by graduates.
SECRET, a. Kept from the knowledge of others, or of all persons except the individuals concerned; private; concealed.
CLOSET, n. A small room or apartment for retirement; any room for privacy.
scriptures: Mat 6:6
But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly.
Mat 6:17
But thou, when thou fastest, anoint thine head, and wash thy face;
Mat 6:18
That thou appear not unto men to fast, but unto thy Father which is in secret: and thy Father, which seeth in secret, shall reward thee openly.
Mat 23:5
But all their works they do for to be seen of men: they make broad their phylacteries, and enlarge the borders of their garments,
corruption_summary: The monk's hood: a garment adopted to conceal devotion that became the most public badge of it — the cowl does not make the monk.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the reversal already described, and Christ had taught against it before the first cowl was cut. “That thou appear not unto men to fast, but unto thy Father which is in secret: and thy Father, which seeth in secret, shall reward thee openly” (Mat 6:18) names both the rule and the reason. A hood that announces a man is fasting has defeated the hood's own purpose, and the proverb about the cowl and the monk is the people's own verdict on the result.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is secret devotion. “pray to thy Father which is in secret” (Mat 6:6) is harder than any rule of dress, because a closed door still leaves a man able to tell others he was behind it, and most of us do.
roots_summary: Latin cucullus, a hood; Greek kruptos (G2927), hidden; Greek tameion (G5009), an inner chamber; Hebrew sether (H5643), a covering or secret place; Greek kalumma (G2571), a veil.
roots_lines: Latin cucullus — a hood or cap; the direct ancestor of the English word.
Greek kruptos (G2927) — hidden, secret; “thy Father, which seeth in secret” (Mat 6:18).
Greek tameion (G5009) — an inner storeroom; “enter into thy closet” (Mat 6:6).
Hebrew sether (H5643) — a covering, a hiding place; the Psalter's secret place of the Most High.
Greek kalumma (G2571) — a veil; the New Testament uses it of what obscures understanding, not of piety.
usage: “when thou hast shut thy door” (Mat 6:6) — the concealment the cowl imitated and then betrayed.
“anoint thine head, and wash thy face” (Mat 6:17) — devotion deliberately not signalled.
“all their works they do for to be seen of men” (Mat 23:5) — the fate of every holy garment.

pos: n. (two strips of cloth worn over the shoulders as part of a habit; in later devotion, a small badge credited with spiritual privileges)
etymology: Latin scapulae, the shoulder blades; the scapular is the shoulder-cloth, originally a working apron to protect the tunic.
biblical_def: The scapular began as a working garment: two panels of cloth joined over the shoulders, worn by monks to keep the tunic clean at labour. As part of a habit it is unremarkable, and its origin in manual work is a point in its favour — the Benedictine houses prayed and dug, and “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10) was a rule they took literally. What is not unremarkable is what the scapular became. In the later Middle Ages a miniature version, two inch-wide squares of brown cloth on cords, was given to lay people with an attached promise, the so-called Sabbatine privilege, of deliverance from purgatory for those who died wearing it. That is where the matter stops being a question of dress and becomes a question of the gospel. A piece of cloth cannot secure salvation; no object can. “Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved” (Act 4:12), and “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8). A badge with a promise attached is an amulet, whatever is embroidered on it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines scapular as pertaining to the shoulder or shoulder blade, and as a noun a part of the habit of certain religious orders; and amulet as something worn as a remedy or preservative against evils or mischief.
webster_full: SCAPULAR, a. Pertaining to the shoulder, or to the scapula; as the scapular arteries.
SCAPULARY, n. A part of the habit of certain religious orders in the Romish church, consisting of two bands of woolen cloth over the shoulders.
AMULET, n. Something worn appended to the neck or body, as a remedy or preservative against evils or mischief, such as diseases and witchcraft.
SUPERSTITION, n. Excessive exactness or rigor in religious opinions or practice; extreme and unnecessary scruples; also, false religion; false worship.
SHOULDER, n. The joint by which the arm of an animal is connected with the body; also, the upper joint of the fore leg.
scriptures: For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.
Act 4:12
Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
And the residue thereof he maketh a god, even his graven image: he falleth down unto it, and worshippeth it, and prayeth unto it, and saith, Deliver me; for thou art my god.
corruption_summary: A monk's working shoulder-cloth that became a badge credited with escaping purgatory: a garment turned amulet, which is idolatry in cloth.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption here is not a matter of degree but of kind. To wear a thing in order to be saved by it is what Scripture calls idolatry, and Isaiah's mockery of the man who makes a god of his own material fits the case uncomfortably well: “he falleth down unto it, and worshippeth it, and prayeth unto it, and saith, Deliver me; for thou art my god” (Isa 44:17). The cloth does not become innocent because the devotion attached to it is sincere. “there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved” (Act 4:12) excludes every object, relic and badge by name.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that salvation is by Christ received by faith and is attached to nothing material whatever — “and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8). Protestants who keep bracelets, tokens and verses-on-objects as quiet insurance should hear this said to them and not only to Rome.
roots_summary: Latin scapulae, shoulder blades; Hebrew shekem (H7926), the shoulder; Greek soteria (G4991), salvation; Greek eidolon (G1497), an idol; Greek charis (G5485), grace.
roots_lines: Latin scapulae — the shoulder blades; the garment is named simply for where it sits.
Hebrew shekem (H7926) — shoulder; in Scripture what bears a burden or a government, never what saves.
Greek soteria (G4991) — salvation; “Neither is there salvation in any other” (Act 4:12).
Greek eidolon (G1497) — an idol, an image; the category a cloth with a promise falls into.
Greek charis (G5485) — grace; “For by grace are ye saved through faith” (Eph 2:8).
usage: “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10) — the labour the garment was originally for.
“Deliver me; for thou art my god” (Isa 44:17) — the prayer an amulet invites.
“there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved” (Act 4:12) — the exclusion that settles it.

pos: n. (a body of lay affiliates attached to a mendicant order under a mitigated rule; the Tertiaries)
etymology: Latin tertius ordo, the third order — after the friars (first) and the enclosed sisters (second); hence tertiary, one of the third.
biblical_def: A Third Order is the lay branch of a mendicant family: men and women living in their own households, keeping their trades and marriages, but bound to a mitigated rule of prayer, fasting, plain dress and works of mercy. The Franciscan Third Order, founded in 1221, became enormous, and in several Italian cities the Tertiaries were the real engine of charity. Their existence is evidence of something healthy and something sick at once. Healthy, because ordinary believers wanted a serious Christian life and would not be content with spectating. Sick, because the church they belonged to had taught them that seriousness lived behind a wall, so that the only form their hunger could take was affiliation to somebody else's rule. Scripture gives the better answer and gives it to everyone. The household is itself the place of discipleship — “thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way” (Deu 6:7) — and the trade is itself the service of God: “let every man, wherein he is called, therein abide with God” (1Co 7:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines order as a religious fraternity or body of men united by some common rule; third as the ordinal of three; and fraternity as a brotherhood, a society or body of men associated.
webster_full: ORDER, n. A religious fraternity; as the order of Benedictines; a body of men united by some common bond or rule.
THIRD, a. The first after the second; the ordinal of three; as, the third hour.
FRATERNITY, n. A brotherhood; a society or body of men associated for their common interest or pleasure.
LAITY, n. The people, as distinguished from the clergy; the body of the people not in orders.
MITIGATE, v.t. To alleviate, as suffering; to abate or lessen the severity of; to soften in severity or harshness.
scriptures: Deu 6:7
And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
Brethren, let every man, wherein he is called, therein abide with God.
Col 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
corruption_summary: The lay branch under a softened rule: a real hunger for serious discipleship, answered by a third tier instead of by the sufficiency of baptism.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the tiering, and it is worth naming precisely because the people in the third tier were often the best Christians in the city. A system that ranks the cloister first, the convent second and the believing household third has inverted Scripture, which gives the household the honour and the commands. “But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people” (1Pe 2:9) is said to the whole church, and it is the end of ranks.

The modern Protestant form is the discipleship tier — a programme, covenant or inner group whose members are the committed and against whom everyone else is measured. The principle to recover is that the ordinary believing life, fully lived, is the serious Christian life: “whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23) has no higher option above it.
roots_summary: Latin tertius ordo, third order; Greek laos (G2992), a people; Greek oikos (G3624), a household; Greek klesis (G2821), a calling; Greek genos (G1085), a kindred or generation.
roots_lines: Latin tertius ordo — the third order; the rank itself, and the problem with it.
Greek laos (G2992) — a people; in the New Testament the laity are the people of God, not a lower grade.
Greek oikos (G3624) — a house or household; the unit Scripture charges with discipleship.
Greek klesis (G2821) — a calling; “let every man, wherein he is called, therein abide with God” (1Co 7:24).
Greek genos (G1085) — a kindred, race, generation; “ye are a chosen generation” (1Pe 2:9).
usage: “let every man, wherein he is called, therein abide with God” (1Co 7:24) — the answer to the hunger the Third Orders met.
“when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way” (Deu 6:7) — discipleship located in the household.
“a royal priesthood, an holy nation” (1Pe 2:9) — the laity's own dignity, needing no affiliation.
